text:
Verse 1

In the name of Allah, the Beneficent, the Merciful.

Sūrahal-Isrāʾ (The Night Journey) was revealed in Mecca and consists of 111 verses.

The chapter relates to God’s unity and His having no partner whatsoever, with the aspect of glorification (tasbīḥ) outweighing that of praise

(taḥmīd). This is seen at the onset of the chapter: Glory be to Him Who made His servant… and is seen time and again later on: Glory be to Him and exalted be He in high exaltation above what they say (17:43); Say: Glory be to my Lord (17:93); And they say: Glory be to our Lord! (17:108). Even the last verse of the chapter praises God while freeing Him from having a partner, guardian or son: And say:(All) praise is due to Allah, Who

has not taken a son and Who has not a partner in the kingdom, and Who has not a guardian to save Him from disgrace; and proclaim His greatness m agnifying (Him ) (17:111).

The chapter is Meccan as the content of the verses show. Rūḥ al-maʿānī says that according to some exegetes, two of its verses are an exception to this: And surely they had purposed to turn you away from… (17:73); And surely they purposed to unsettle you from the land… (17:76).

Others have added two more verses to the exception: And when We said to you: Surely your Lord encompasses men… (17:60); And say: My Lord! make me to enter a goodly entering… (17:80).

According to al-Ḥasan, it is Meccan except for five of its verses: And do not kill any one… (17:33); And go not nigh to adultery… (17:32); Those whom they call upon… (17:57); Keep up prayer… (17:78); And give to the near of kin… (17:26).

On the authority of Muqātil, it is Meccan except for the following five verses: And surely they had purposed to turn you away… (17:73); And surely they purposed to unsettle you from the land… (17:76); And when We said to you:… (17:60); And say: My Lord! make me to enter… (17:80); …surely those who are given the knowledge before it… (17:107).

According to Qatādah and al-Muʿaddil on the authority of Ibn ʿAbbās: It is Meccan except for eight verses: And surely they had purposed to turn you away… And say: My Lord! make me to enter a goodly entering…

(17:73-80).

However, the content and themes of the verses themselves bear no indication of the chapter being Medinite, and none of its laws relate to things that were exclusively revealed in Medina. Rather, similar laws were revealed in Meccan chapters such as Chapters 6 and 7 (al-Anʿām and al-Aʿrāf).

The chapter begins with its theme of glorifying God by alluding to the Prophet’s ascension (miʿrāj). It mentions his nocturnal journey (isrāʾ) from the Sacred Mosque to the Farthest Mosque which is Jerusalem (Bayt al-Maqdis). This is the temple that was built by David and Solomon, and which was sanctified by God for the Israelites.

This is then linked to the rise, fall, honor and dishonor decreed by God for the Israelites. W henever they obeyed, God raised them up, and whenever they disobeyed God put them down. He revealed the Book to them,

commanded them to monotheism and prohibited them from polytheism. He then turns the discourse to the state of this nation and the Book that has been sent to them, which is similar to the case of the Israelites; if the Muslims obey they will be rewarded, and if they disobey they will be punished. It is only a matter of one’s actions, for every individual is treated according to what he does. Thus was the divine tradition with regard to past nations.

It then refers to many truths pertaining to knowledge of the origin, the resurrection, general religious laws including commands and prohibitions, and so on.

Some cardinal verses (ghurar al-āyāt) in this chapter are: Say: Call upon Allah or call upon, the Beneficent God; whichever you call upon, He has the best names (17:110); All do We aid – these as well as those – out of the bounty of your Lord, and the bounty of your Lord is not confined (17:20);

And there is not a town but We will destroy it… (17:58), and more.

Commentary

(17:1) Glory be to Him (subḥān) Who made His servant to go (asrā) on a night (laylan) from the Sacred Mosque to the remote mosque of which We have blessed the precincts, so that We may show to him some of Our signs; surely He is the Hearing, the Seeing. Subḥān is the verbal noun of tasbīḥ, which means to affirm the transcendence of something (tanzīh). It is used annexed to a noun (muḍāfan)

as an absolute object (mafʿūl muṭlaq) that takes the place of a verb. The implied meaning of subḥān Allāh is: subḥān Allāh is sabbaḥtu Allāha tasbīḥan, meaning “I declare God’s freedom from everything inappropriate to His Holiness.” This phrase is often used as an exclamation.

However the context of these verses only fits glorification, because that is the theme of the discourse, even though some exegetes have insisted that it is exclamatory.

Isrāʾ and sary mean travelling at night. Sarā asrā means that he travelled at night. Sarā usriya bihi means that he was taken on a journey at

night. Another similar term is sayr (travel), which is used only for daytime and night time.

Laylan is a locative object. It means that this journey took place at night and that the round-trip took place in a single night before dawn broke.

…to the Farthest Mosque (al-Masjid al-Aqṣā) of which We have blessed the precincts…: To the Farthest Mosque means Jerusalem, as indicated by: of which We have blessed the precincts. Qaṣā means remoteness. It is called the Farthest Mosque (al-Masjid al-Aqṣā) because it was

the Farthest Mosque from the Sacred Mosque in Mecca, which was the position of the Prophet and the other addressees with him.

…so that We may show to him some of Our signs …: This explains the purpose of the night journey: to show him some of the divine signs— the particle min means “some of.” The context of the verse indicates the greatness of these signs which God showed to the Prophet. This meaning is explicitly stated elsewhere in the Qur’an when discussing the story of the night journey: Certainly he saw of the greatest signs of his Lord (53:18).

…surely He is the Hearing, the Seeing: This explains why He made him journey by night in order to shown him His signs: It was because He hears what His servants say and sees what they do. He heard what His servant said, and He saw that his inner state and condition (ḥāl) called for being distinguished [from others] with the honor of being taken on a nocturnal journey and seeing some of His greatest signs.

…Of which We have blessed the precincts, so that We may show to him some of Our signs: Here we see a grammatical shifiifor rhetorical purpose from the third person to the first person plural, which is then followed by a

returns to the previous third person. The reason for this shifiiis to indicate

that the night journey and what happened there—showing the signs to the Prophet—issued from the courtyard of grandeur and greatness, and the position of might and power. This was an act of God’s greatest authority, where He manifested Himself (tajallā) to him through His greatest signs. If the verse had said, “To show him of His signs” or anything else, this subtle point would not have been made.1

The implied meaning is: One must thoroughly clear and glorify the One Who made His servant Muḥammad travel in the middle of a single night from the Sacred Mosque to the Farthest Mosque in Jerusalem— the precincts of which He had blessed—to show him His greatest signs through His greatness and grandeur and by His far-reaching power and authority. He did this because He is the Hearing, the Seeing. He knew that his servant is worthy of being distinguished by this honor based on what He heard of his supplication and of what He saw of his inner condition. Examining Narrations

(1) Imam al-Ṣādiq said:

Gabriel (Jabraʾīl), Michael (Mīkāʾīl) and Seraphiel (Isrāfīl) brought the burāq2 to God’s Messenger, one taking the rein, another the stirrups and the other spreading his clothing over it. There the burāq startled, so Gabriel slapped it and said to it, “Calm down, burāq, because no prophet like he has ever ridden you nor will ever ride you.”

1 This is because “Our” is a majestic plural or the royal “We.” (Trans.)

2 This is a heavenly mount that carried the Prophet on his night journey. (Trans.)

It then fiew him and lifted him up not too high, accompanied by Gabriel who showed him the signs of heaven and the earth.

He [the Prophet] said: While I was looking to the lef , someone called out from my right: “O Muḥammad!” I did not answer him or turn toward him. Someone then called me from my lef : “O Muḥammad!” but I did not answer him or turn toward him. A woman then faced me, her forearms exposed, upon which was all the world’s finery. She said: “O Muḥammad, look at me so that I can speak to you,” but I did not turn toward her. I travelled on and then I heard a voice that frightened me, but I kept going. Thereafter, Gabriel put me down and said: “Pray,” so I prayed. He then asked: “Do you know where you prayed?” I replied: “No.”

He said, “You prayed on Mount Sinai where God spoke directly to Moses.”

I mounted and we travelled as far as God willed, then he [Gabriel] said to me: “Dismount and pray,” so I dismounted and prayed.

He then asked me, “Do you know where you prayed?” I replied, “No.” He said, “You have prayed in Bethlehem. Bethlehem is in the district of Jerusalem where Jesus son of Mary was born.”

I then mounted and we travelled until we reached Jerusalem.

There I tied up the burāq to the ring where the prophets used to tie their steeds. Gabriel was by my side. We then found Abraham, Moses and Jesus among a group of Prophets that only God knows their count. They gathered around me and the iqāmah was recited for prayer. I had no doubt that Gabriel would lead us but then when they straightened their lines Gabriel took my arms, led me ahead [of himself], and thus I led their congregation. There is no boast in that.

The treasurer then brought me three cups: there was milk in one, water in another, and wine in the third. I heard someone say: “If he takes water, he and his nation will drown. If he takes wine, he and his nation will go astray. If he takes milk, he and his nation will be guided.” So I took the milk and drank from it. Thereafter, Gabriel said to me: “You have gone aright and your nation will go aright.” He then asked me: “What did you see in your journey?” I replied: “Someone called to me from my right.” He then asked me, “Did you answer him?” I said, “No, nor did I turn toward him.” He said, “That was the Jewish proselytizer. If you had answered him, your nation would have turned Jewish after you.” He then said, “What did you see [then]?” I replied, “Someone called to me from my lef .” He asked me, “Did you answer him?” I replied, “No, nor did I turn toward him.” So he replied, “That was the Christian proselytizer. If you had answered him, your nation would have become Christian after you.” He then asked, “What faced you?” I replied, “I met a woman, exposing her forearms which bore all of the world’s finery. She said, ‘O Muḥammad!

Look at me so that I can talk to you.’” He asked, “Did you speak to her?” I replied, “I neither spoke to her nor turned toward her.” He said, “That was the world (dunyā). If you had spoken to her, your nation would have chosen this world over the hereafter.” I then heard a voice, which frightened me and so Gabriel, asked me, “Do you hear, Muḥammad?” I replied, “Yes.” He said, “This is a rock that I cast from the edge of hell seventy years ago and now it reached the bottom.”

It has been said that after this incident the Messenger of God did not laugh until he passed away.1

He [the Prophet] said: Gabriel ascended and I ascended with him to the lowest heaven, which is guarded by an angel called Ismāʿīl. He fends offthe snatchers as mentioned in the verse: Except him who snatches offbut once, then there follows him a brightly shining flame (37:10). There are seventy thousand angels under him

and under every angel there are another seventy thousand angels. He [Ismāʿīl] asked, “O Gabriel! Who is this who is with you?”

Gabriel replied: “It is Muḥammad, the Messenger of God.” He asked: “Has he been sent [to his people] yet?” He replied: “Yes.” He then opened the door, I greeted him and he greeted me. I sought forgiveness for him and he sought forgiveness for me. He said: “Welcome to the righteous brother and prophet.”

The angels kept coming to meet me until I entered the lowest heaven. They all received me while smiling with delight until I was received by an angel that was greater than anything that I had ever seen, with an unpleasant countenance, and visibly angry.

He said the same prayer for me as the others angels, except that

1 This is an aside statement by Imam al-Ṣādiq—or one of the transmitters of the hadith—in his narration of the Prophet’s night journey. (Trans.) he did not smile and I did not see the delight of the other angels in him. I asked: “Who is this, Gabriel? Indeed I am terrified of him.” He replied: “It makes sense to be terrified of him—we are all terrified of him—because this is Mālik, the custodian of hell. He has never laughed and has remained so ever since God put him in charge of hell. He gets angrier and more infuriated every day at God’s enemies and the people of disobedience, for God takes revenge on them through him. If he were to smile at anyone ever, it would have been you.” I then greeted him. He greeted me back and gave me glad tidings of heaven. Since God has described Gabriel’s position as: One (to be) obeyed, and faithful in trust

(81:21) I asked him [Gabriel]: “Will you not tell him to show me hell?” So Gabriel said to him: “O Mālik! Show Muḥammad hell.”

He uncovered it to me and opened one of its gates. A flame blazed out in the sky from it, fiared up and rose until I thought that it is going to catch me. I said: “Gabriel! Tell him to cover it up again.” He told him and he said to the fire: “Go back!” It then returned to its place from which it had come.

I then passed onwards and saw a large bodied swarthy man (rajulan ādaman).1 I asked: “Who is this, Gabriel?” He said: “This is

your forefather Adam, where he is shown his offsprings and he says: Good spirit and good fragrance from a good body.”

God’s Messenger then recited Chapter 83 (Sūrah al-Muṭaffīn)

from after verse 17: Nay! Most surely the record of the righteous shall be in theIliyin. And what will make you know what the highest Iliyin is? It is a written book, those who are drawn near (to Allah) shall witness it (83:18-21) to the end of the chapter.

He [the Prophet] said: I greeted my forefather Adam and he greeted me. I sought forgiveness for him and he sought forgiveness for me. He said: “Greetings to the righteous son and the

righteous prophet sent in the righteous time.”

He said: I then passed by one of the angels sitting on a seat (majlis). The whole of the world was between his knees a tablet of

light with some writing was in his hand. He was looking at the tablet with fixed eyes, without turning to the right or the lef , and

1 The Arabic terms in brackets are what the author has discussed and defined after the tradition. (Trans.)

his face looked like an aggrieved person. I asked: “Who is this, Gabriel?” He said: “This is the angel of death, who is relentless in capturing the souls.” I said: “Gabriel, take me close to him so that I can speak to him.” He took me close to him, I greeted him and Gabriel said to him: “This is Muḥammad, the Prophet of Mercy whom God has sent to His servants.” He welcomed me, prayed for my longevity in peace, and said: “Rejoice, O Muḥammad, for indeed I see that all good is in your nation.” I said: “Praise be to God, the Benefactor, Who has blessed His servants with bounties. This is of my Lord’s blessing and mercy upon me.” Gabriel then said: “He is the most hardworking angel.” I asked him [the Angel of Death]: “Are you the one who has taken the life of everyone who has ever died or will ever die from now on?” He replied:

“Yes.” I asked: “Do you see them wherever they are and witness them by yourself?” He replied: “Yes.” The angel of death then added: “God has placed the entire universe under my authority and power just like a dirham in the hand of a person, where he can fiip it as he pleases. There is not a single home which I do not peruse five times every day. I say when the family of a deceased weeps over the deceased: Do not cry for him because I will keep visiting you over and over again until none of you shall remain.” God’s Messenger then said: “Death is enough of an overwhelming catastrophe (ṭāmmah), O Gabriel.” Gabriel replied: “And what

comes after death is a much greater catastrophe than death.”

He [the Prophet] said: I then passed onwards, and lo, I reached a group of people in front of whom were tables spread with good meat and bad meat. They were eating from the bad meat and leaving the good meat untouched. I asked: “Who are these, Gabriel?”

He replied: “They are those who eat what is unlawful instead of what is lawful. They are from your nation, O Muḥammad.”

God’s Messenger continued: I then saw an angel whom God had created in an astonishing fashion: half of his body was fire and the other half was ice. The fire did not melt the ice and the ice did not extinguish the fire. He was calling out in a loud voice, saying: “Praise be to Him Who has stopped the heat of this fire from melting the ice, and has stopped the cold of this ice from extinguishing the heat of this fire. O God, binder of fire to ice, bind together the hearts of your believing servants.” I asked: “Who is this, Gabriel?” He replied: “This is an angel whom God has put in charge of the sides (aknāf) of heaven[s] and the edges of the earths. He is the sincerest adviser of God’s angels for His believing servants among the people of the earth. He has been praying for them as you heard since he was created.”

I saw two angels calling out in heaven; one of them was saying: “O God, compensate anyone who gives charity”; and the other one was saying: “O God, bring loss to anyone who withholds [from donation].”

I then passed onwards, and lo, I reached a group of people who had lips like that of camels. Their flesh was being cut from their sides and cast into their mouths. I asked: “Who are these, Gabriel?” He replied: “They are those who slander and backbite others.”

I then passed onwards, and lo, I reached a group of people smashing their heads with rocks. I asked: “Who are they, Gabriel?”

He replied: “They are those who sleep without performing the Evening Prayer (ṣalāt al-ʿishāʾ).”

I then passed onwards, and lo, I reached a group of people where fire was being cast in their mouths and was exiting through their bottoms. I asked: “W ho are they, Gabriel?” He replied: “They are those who eat what belongs to the orphans unjustly. Surely they only swallow fire into their bellies and soon they shall enter burning fire [4:10].”

I then passed onwards, and lo, I reached a group of people that wanted to stand up but could not because their stomachs were too big. I asked: “Who are they, Gabriel?” He replied: “They are: Those who swallow down usury cannot arise except as one whom Satan has prostrated by (his) touch does rise (2:275).” They were treated as Pharaoh’s family, exposed to the fire (every) morning and evening [40:46], saying: Lord, when will the hour come?

I then passed onwards and lo, I was beside women hung by their breasts. I asked: “W ho are these, Gabriel?” He replied: “They are those who pass on their husbands’ inheritance to children who are not their husbands’.”

The Messenger of God said:1 “God’s wrath is severe at a woman

1 Based on the Arabic text of the hadith, apparently this is an aside statement

who introduces an outsider to a family’s lineage, that he may discover their fiaws and weak spots and consume their treasures.”

He then said: We passed by some of God’s angels whom God had created as He pleased and had set their faces as He pleased. There was no spot on their bodies that was not praising and glorifying God from every side in various voices. Their voices rose in praise and weeping in awe of God. I asked Gabriel about them, and he replied: “They were created as you can see. Surely every angel out of them does not speak a word to his counterpart next to him, nor do they raise their heads to what is above them or lower [their heads] to what is beneath them out of fear of God and humility [toward Him].” I then greeted them and they signaled a greeting back to me by nodding their heads and without looking at me, out of humility [toward God]. Gabriel then said to them: “This is Muḥammad, the prophet of Mercy, sent by God to His servants as a messenger and prophet. He is the last of the prophets and their master. Are you not going to speak to him?” When they heard this from Gabriel, they faced me, greeted me with honor, and gave me glad tidings of goodness for me and my nation.

We then ascended to the second heaven, and lo, there were two men there who looked like each other. I asked: “Who are they, Gabriel?” He replied to me: “Maternal cousins John [the Baptist] and Jesus.” I greeted them and they greeted me. I sought forgiveness for them and they sought forgiveness for me. They said:

“Greetings to the righteous brother and prophet.”

There [in the second heaven] I also saw angels who had [signs of] humility upon them. God had fashioned their faces as He pleased. There was no angel among them except that it was glorifying and praising God in different voices.

We then ascended to the third heaven, and lo, there was a man who exceeded the rest of creation in beauty, the way the full moon exceeds the rest of the stars [in brightness]. I asked: “W ho is this, Gabriel?” He replied: “This is your brother Joseph.” I greeted him and he greeted me. I sought forgiveness for him and he sought forgiveness for me. He said: “Welcome to the righteous prophet that the Prophet made when narrating his night journey, not something that he said during the journey. (Trans.)

and the righteous brother sent in the righteous time.” There [in the third heaven] I also saw angels who had [signs of] humility upon them like the ones I described in the first and second heavens. Gabriel told them about me what he had said to the others

and they did as the others had done.

We then ascended to the fourth heaven, and lo, there was a man there. I asked: “W ho is this, Gabriel?” He replied: “This is Enoch (Idrīs), whom God has raised to a high station.” I greeted him and he greeted me. I sought forgiveness for him and he sought forgiveness for me. There [in the fourth heaven] I also saw angels who had [signs of] humility upon them like in the heavens I had passed through. They gave me glad tidings for me and for my nation. I then saw an angel sitting on a couch. He had seventy thousand angels under him, and there were another seventy thousand angels under each of them.

It occurred to God’s Messenger that he was it.1 Gabriel called out to him, saying: “Get up! And thus he will [remain] standing until the Day of Resurrection.”

[The Prophet continued:] We then ascended to the fifth heaven, and lo, there was a middle-aged man with large eyes. I had not seen a middle-aged man greater than him. Around him was a group of his nation. Their multitude impressed me, so I asked: “Who is this, Gabriel?” He replied: “This is the beloved of his people, Aaron son of Amram (ʿImrān).” I greeted him and he greeted me. I sought forgiveness for him and he sought forgiveness for me. I also saw angels there with [signs of] humility upon

them as I had seen in the [other] heavens.

We then ascended to the sixth heaven, and lo, there was a tall, dark-complexioned man, as if he was from Shanuwwah2 [an Arab tribe]. If he were to wear two shirts his hair would have passed through both. I heard him say: “The Israelites claim that I am the

1 The author has described what is meant by this after the hadith. This sentence

again is a statement by Imam al-Ṣādiq. (Trans.)

2 Shanūʾah, also written as Shanuwwah, is the name of an Arab tribe. Some narrations say Shabwah, which is the name of another Arab tribe. Either way, the man is likened to the people of an Arab tribe for his color. Majlisī, Biḥār

al-anwār, 18:332. See the author’s comments after the hadith. (Trans.) dearest son of Adam to God, but this man is dearer to God than I.” I asked: “W ho is this, Gabriel?” He replied: “This is your brother Moses son of Amram (ʿImrān).” I greeted him and he greeted me. I sought forgiveness for him and he sought forgiveness for me. I also saw angels there with [signs of] humility upon them like in the [other] heavens.

We then ascended to the seventh heaven and I did not pass a single angel who did not say: “O Muḥammad! Cup and tell your nation to cup (ḥijāmah).” And lo, there was a grey haired and grey bearded man (ashmaṭ) sitting on a throne there. I asked: “Gabriel, who is this that is in the seventh heaven at the door of al-Bayt al-Maʿmūr (the Frequented House)1 near to God?” He replied:

“This, Muḥammad, is your forefather Abraham, and this is your place and the place of the Godwary in your nation.”

God’s Messenger then recited: “Most surely the nearest of people to Ibrahim are those who followed him and this prophet and those who believe and Allah is the guardian of the believers (3:68).”2 [The Prophet continued]: I greeted him and he greeted me and said: “Welcome to the righteous prophet and the righteous son, sent in the righteous time.” I also saw angels there with [signs of] humility upon them like in the [other] heavens. They gave me glad tidings for me and for my nation.

God’s Messenger said: I saw in the seventh heaven seas of shining bright light, with such glitter that could snatch away one’s sight. There were [also] seas of darkness there and seas of snow that were thundering. Whenever I was appalled and saw something frightening I inquired Gabriel [about it] and he would tell me: “Rejoice, O Muḥammad! Give thanks for your Lord’s blessing upon you, and thank God for what he Has made for you.”

He [the Prophet] said: Thereafter, God made me firm with His strength and help. After speaking much with Gabriel and expressing my astonishment, Gabriel said: “O Muḥammad! Do you think

1 Al-Bayt al-Maʿmūr (the Frequented House, the Inhabited House) is not a terrestrial place of worship, but a heavenly one. See narration 9 under Discussion

of the Narrations below. (Trans.)

2 Again, this is Imam al-Ṣādiq’s narration. Perhaps the Prophet added this verse

when he was recounting the story of his ascension afterwards. (Trans.) what you see is great? This is but one creations of of your Lord’s creations. What about the Creator Who has created what you see? And what you do not see of your Lord’s creation is greater than this. There are seventy thousand veils between God and His creation. I and Seraphiel are the closest creatures to God. Between us and Him are four veils: a veil of light, a veil of darkness, a veil of cloud and a veil of water.”

He [the Prophet] said: Among the wondrous things that God had created and was under His command I saw a rooster whose feet were on the [lowest] limits of the seventh earths and whose head was at the throne. He was one of God’s angels whom God had created as He had willed, with its two feet positioned on the [lowest] limits of the seventh earths. He then started ascending into the air toward the seventh heaven, and continued to ascend to the point that his crown ended up near the throne. He says: “I glorify my Lord wherever I am. Your Lord is of such grand status that you do not know where He is.” He has two wings on his

shoulders. When he spreads them they go past the east and the west. At dawn time, he spreads his wings, fiaps them and cries out the following praise: “Glory be to God, the King, the Holy. Glory be to God, the Great, the Transcendent. There is no god but God, the All-Living, the Upright.” When he says this, all the roosters of the earth fiap their wings and start glorifying God. When that rooster in heaven falls silent, all the roosters in earth fall silent. That rooster had green feathers (zaghab) under his white plumages. The whiteness of the plumage was the brightest white that

I had ever seen, and the green of the underlying feathers was the most intense green that I had ever seen.

I then passed onwards with Gabriel and entered al-Bayt al-Maʿmūr, where I prayed two units (rakʿah) of prayer. With me were some of my companions wearing new clothes, and others wearing ragged clothes. Those wearing new clothes entered, and those wearing ragged clothes sat down [outside].

I then went out and found two rivers flowing before me, one called al-Kawthar (lit. “Abundance of Good”) and another called al-Raḥmah (lit. “Mercy”). I drank from al-Kawthar and washed up from al-Raḥmah. They both opened up the way for me so I entered al-jannah (the Garden, Paradise). Its earth was like musk, and lo, on its two sides were the houses of me and my household (ahlī). There I saw a servant-girl dipping in the Garden’s rivers. I asked her: “To whom do you belong, O servant-girl?” She replied: “To Zayd b. Ḥārithah”—I gave him the glad tidings of her when I woke up in the morning.

Its birds were like Bactrian camels (al-bakht), and its pomegranates were like great buckets (duliyy). There was a tree there that

if a bird were released at its base it could not go round it in seven hundred years. There is not a single home in the Garden which does not have one of its branches in it. I asked: “What is this, Gabriel?” He replied: “This is the Ṭūbā Tree.”

God says: Tuba shall be theirs and a goodly return (13:29).1 God’s Messenger said: When I entered the garden I thought with myself and asked Gabriel about the seas there, their terror and their wonders. He replied: “They are the canopies of veils with which God veils Himself. Were it not for those veils, the light of the Throne would burn everything in it.”

I finally reached the farthest lote-tree (sidrat al-muntahā), and lo, there was a leaf on it which shaded one of the nations. I was as near to it as God says: The measure of two bows or closer still (53:9). He [God] then called out to me: “The Messenger believes in what has been revealed to him from his Lord [2:285].” So I said, responding on behalf of myself and my nation: “and (so do) the believers; they all believe in Allah and His angels and His books and His

messengers; We make no difference between any of His messengers; and they say: We hear and obey, our Lord! Furthermore, the narration itself refutes the idea that the night journey took place before the start of the Prophet’s mission. This is because

it contains the imposition of prayer, initially being fifty, followed by [the

Prophet’s] request for reduction as per Moses’ suggestion. It does not make sense to impose the prayer before the prophetic mission. Therefore, we should perhaps interpret the beginning of the hadith as follows: The angels initially came to him before he received revelation, then they lef him, and then they returned to him another night after he was chosen as a prophet. Some narrations say that those who were sleeping next to him in the Mosque on the night he was taken on the night journey were Ḥamzah b. ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib, and Abū Ṭālib’s sons Jaʿfar and ʿAlī.

As for what it says about its happening in a dream, it might refer— although it is unlikely—only to the story of cleaving open and washing [the heart]. However, the narration apparently suggests that the entire night journey took place in a dream, as also suggested in some narrations below.

A Summary of the Narrations

The reader should know that the narrations mentioned above are just a small sample of the narrations on this topic. They are indeed numerous, reaching the level of tawātur.3 They are broadly transmitted by a very large number of Companions such as Anas b. Mālik, Shaddād b. al-Aws, ʿAlī b. The scholars of Islam—whose word carries weight—agree that the night journey took place in Mecca before the migration, as can be inferred from His words: Glory be to Him Who made His servant to go on a night from the Sacred Mosque… (17:1). This is also confirmed by many narrations that talk about the Prophet telling Quraysh [a Meccan tribe] about

it the morning after that night, their denial of this report, and the Prophet

informing them about the pillars of the Farthest Mosque and what he had encountered on the way like the caravans and so on.

But they disagree over the year in which he was taken on the night journey. The following years have been claimed:

(i) the second year of the mission, on the authority of Ibn ʿAbbās; (ii) the third year, according to al-Kharāʾij [by al-Rāwandī], on the authority of ʿAlī;

(iii) the fifth or sixth year;

(iv) ten years and three months after his appointment [as prophet]; (v) the twelfih year of the mission;

(vi) one year and five months before the migration;

(vii) one year and three months before it;

(viii) six months before it.

Here we are not concerned with discussing the year, month or date of the night journey, and there is no reliable evidence for it either. However, it should be noted that some of the narrations on the authority of the Imams of Ahl al-Bayt explicitly state that there were two night journeys. This can be inferred from the verses in Chapter 53 because He says: And certainly he saw him in another descent (53:13). You will see this when we get there, God-willing.

Based on this, it is possible that some of the marvels that he described in some of the narrations refer to what he witnessed on the first night journey, some others refer to the second night journey, and some refer to what he witnessed on both night journeys.

The exegetes have also disagreed over the place from which he was taken on the night journey. The following origins have been claimed: (i) From the shiʿb (mountain pass) of Abū Ṭālib.

(ii) From Umm Hānī’s house, and there are some narrations that confirm this.

[Concerning these two views] some exegetes have interpreted “the Sacred Mosque” in verse 17:1 (…made His servant to go on a night from the Sacred Mosque) as referring to the entire ḥaram area (the holy precinct) by extension, which would include all of Mecca.

(iii) From the Sacred Mosque itself, as this is the literal meaning of the verse, and there is no evidence to support an extension or figurative interpretation (taʾwīl) of it.

Based on what we said above—that there were two night journeys—it is possible that one of the night journeys was from the Sacred Mosque and the other was from Umm Hānī’s house. As for its happening from the mountain pass [of Abū Ṭalib], it does not comply with the rest of what is said in these accounts, as they say that Abū Ṭālib was looking for the Prophet all night, he and the Hāshimites (Banū Hāshim) gathered together in the Sacred Mosque, and he drew his sword and threatened Quraysh about not finding the Prophet, until he descended from heaven, went to them and told Quraysh what he had seen. None of these fit the hardship and suffering he and the Hāshimites all underwent while they were on the mountain pass.

In any event, the night journey discussed in the verse: Glory be to Him Who made His servant to go on a night from the Sacred Mosque to the Farthest Mosque (17:1) was a night journey to Bayt al-Maqdis, and this started at the Sacred Mosque because that is perfectly apparent from the verse, and there is no need to interpret it figuratively.

The exegetes also disagree over how the nocturnal journey took place. The majority believe that his body and spirit were taken on the night journey from the Sacred Mosque to Bayt al-Maqdis, then from there to the heavens. A number of them believe that his body and soul were taken from Mecca to Bayt al-Maqdis, then his spirit was taken from Bayt al-Maqdis to the heavens. It is attributed to some exegetes that only his spirit was taken on the journey, meaning that it was a true dream that God showed His prophet.

Allāh took him up to Himself… (4:158); Idrīs’ (Enoch’s) to heaven: And We raised him high [in Heaven] (19:57); and Muḥammad’s to the measure of two bows or closer still (53:9). This shows his [Muḥammad’s] lofty purpose and will.

What should be said is that there is no way to deny the actual occurrence of the night journey because the Qur’an refers to it explicitly and

there are repeatedly narrated traditions about it by the Prophet and the Imams of Ahl al-Bayt.

As for the quality of the night journey (isrāʾ), the verse, the narrations and their contextual and circumstantial indications are a clear evidence that both his spirit and his body were taken from the Sacred Mosque to the Farthest Mosque. Concerning his ascension (miʿrāj) to the heaven, this is also evident based on the verses in Chapter 53—the exegesis of which is to come, God-willing—and the explicit text of numerous narrations. However, one may say that this ascension [to the heaven, after the physical night journey to Bayt al-Maqdis] was a spiritual ascension, but not in the sense suggested by those who have deemed to be as a form of dreams or visions that one sees in sleep. If that were the case, it would neither justify

the ascension being a sign of God’s power and esteem [of His prophet], as stated in the verses, nor would it justify Quraysh’s strong denial when he told them the story. In addition, what he told them of the events along the way would have no conceivable meaning. Rather, a correct interpretation of a spiritual ascension is that his noble spirit was taken to a realm

beyond the material world, inhabited by honored angels, where deeds end up and from which God’s decrees issue. He then saw some of his Lords greatest signs (53:18) and the manifestation of the realities of things and the consequences of deeds. He saw the spirits of the greatest prophets and spoke with them, and he met the noble angels and conversed with them. He also saw divine signs that are only metaphorically describable such as the Throne, the veil (al-ḥujub) and the pavilions (al-surādiqāt). Since most scholars hold that immaterial existence is restricted to God, and that others are subject to the primacy of material existence, when they find the Qur’an and Sunnah describe immaterial matters in terms of specific tangible bodies or entities—such as the noble angels, the Throne, the Chair, the Tablet, the Pen, the veils and the pavilions—they have construed them as being material bodies that are imperceptible to the senses and free from the laws of matter. They have also interpreted what is said about the representations of the stations of the pious, the degrees of proximity, the hidden forms of sins, the consequences of deeds and so on as allegorical and metaphorical expressions. Thus they have fallen into sophistry by invalidating sensory perception, confirming arbitrary links between deeds and their consequences, and other pitfalls.

It is for the same reason that those scholars who have denied his material ascension to the heavens are forced to say that his ascension occurred

in a dream, which, according to them, is a material property of the spirit— because they deem the spirit to also be material. Thus they have been led to reinterpret the verses and narrations as what is not appropriate to even a single one of them.

Another Discussion

Majmaʿ al-bayān says:

One question is about where the Prophet was taken on the night journey. The answer is that the night journey was to Bayt alMaqdis. This is explicitly stated in the Qur’an, and no Muslim can deny it. What some exegetes have said—that it happened in sleep—is clearly untrue because that would serve as no miracle or binding proof.

There are many narrations telling the story of our Prophet’s ascension to heaven, narrated by many of the companions such as

Ibn ʿAbbās, Ibn Masʿūd, Anas, Jābir b. ʿAbd-Allāh, Ḥudhayfah, ʿĀʾishah, Umm Hānī and others, who have narrated from the Prophet. Some say more and some say less.

W hat is said in these narrations can be classified into four categories:

(i) That which we can be certain of its authenticity due to having knowledge about them and their being mass-transmitted.

(ii) That which is rationally possible and does not contradict the established principles (ūsūl). We believe in the possibility of these, and if they happened they were while he was awake, not in sleep. (iii) That which apparently contravenes some principles, but there can be a logical interpretation for it. It is possible to interpret it non-literally in a way which conforms to the truth and evidence. (iv) That which is apparently not correct and which cannot be interpreted plausibly except with a lot of difficulty and abstraction from the apparent meaning. It is better not to accept it.

What is of the first type—that which is definitive—is that overall he was taken on a night journey. The second type includes narrations that he circumambulated the heavens, saw the prophets,

the Throne, the farthest lote-tree, heaven, hell and so on. Some examples for the third type are narrations that he saw people living at ease in heaven and people in hell being punished there. This should be interpreted as seeing their attributes or names. The fourth type includes narrations that he literally spoke to God and saw Him [with the naked eye], sat with Him on His couch and so on, because the literal meanings of these necessitate anthropomorphism. God is far above that. Similarly there are narrations that his inside was split open and cleansed. These are also

of the fourth type because he was already pure and cleansed of every evil and defect. Moreover, how can his heart and beliefs be cleansed by water?

Author’s comment: His categorisation is appropriate. However, there is room for discussion over most of the examples he cites corresponding to the categories.

What he says about the circumambulation, seeing the prophets and so on are imaginal or spiritual representations (tamaththulāt barzakhiyyah aw rūḥiyyah). Similarly the hadith about his inside being split open and cleansed is an imaginal representation, and there is no problem with it. The hadiths on the night journey are full of reference to this kind of imagery, like the world being represented as a woman covered in all the world’s finery, the representation of the Jewish and Christian proselytizers, the kinds of comfort and punishment he saw for the people of heaven and hell, respectively, and so on.

This view of ours is confirmed by the difference of expression in these narrations despite depicting the same reality. For example, one narration says that he ascended to heaven on the burāq, another on Gabriel’s wing, and another via a stairway set up on Bayt al-Maqdis’ rock. There are other examples of this that one can find by scrutinizing these narrations. These and others like them point to the fact that such explanations are set out as imagery or figurative representations. The occurrence of such imagery in the apparent text of the Qur’an and Sunnah is certain and cannot be denied by any means.
